en: The Transmission of the Dharma-treasury through its Causes and Conditions, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Ki-carya of the Western Regions during the Yuan Wei Dynasty, together with Tanyao.
Homage to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, who are boundless.
The Immovable Wisdom Equal to Space, the World-Savior, the Great Compassionate Honored One—
formerly, the Bhagavān sought the most supreme path for the sake of sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas.
He accomplished various difficult practices and ascetic austerities,
relinquishing his beloved body— its head, eyes, marrow, and brain— as well as his kingdom, cities, wife, children, palaces, ministers, and concubines;
he cast himself from cliffs, leaped into fire, and had his body cut and severed.

At times, for the sake of a single four-line verse, one might flay one's skin to serve as paper, break one's bones to serve as pens, and use one's blood as ink to transcribe, honor, study under an enlightened teacher, and receive the teachings of the Buddhas.
Compassionate toward the multitude of sentient beings, he accumulated merit through tireless humility;
he cultivated myriad virtuous deeds and gave rise to great vows,
as is explained in detail in the five hundred Jātaka tales.
Having perfected his fundamental training and being on the verge of attaining perfect enlightenment,
he sat cross-legged beneath the Bodhi tree; at that time,
the sixth celestial Māra gave rise to deep anguish and malice.
Reflecting that once he had attained the Way, he would surely surpass him,
he immediately led his officials and subordinates, numbering eighteen trillion,
to the foot of the King of Trees and said to the Bodhisattva:
"You should now rise quickly and return to the palace.
If you do not, I shall seize your feet and hurl you beyond the great ocean."
At that time, the Bodhisattva, like a lion king, with a mind free from alarm or fear,
addressed him, saying: "Pāpīyan!"
In the past, you once made offerings to a pratyekabuddha and observed the eightfold precepts;
by virtue of this merit, you have become a heavenly king.
However, I have [practiced] for incalculable kalpas.
I have fully accomplished difficult and ascetic practices;
there is not even a space as small as the point of a needle upon the great earth that was not a place where I practiced austerities in the past.
Even if the hosts of Māra were as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
"You cannot move even a single hair of mine.
How is it that you now wish to hurl my body beyond the great ocean?
Māra spoke again, saying:
That in the past I bestowed gifts upon a pratyekabuddha and thereby attained the status of a celestial king—
this matter can be clearly demonstrated.
As for what you have now said, by what means do you provide proof?
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva extended his hand and pointed to the earth,
saying, "This deity knows me.
At that moment, the Earth Deity emerged from the adamantine foundation, rising up from within the earth.
Joining his palms, he said:
"Truly, as Your Reverence has taught;
since I have been here from the beginning, I have served as its deity."
In this place, there is not even a space as small as the point of a needle that is not a site for the fundamental practice of a bodhisattva.
When Māra heard these words,
he fell down in a state of total confusion.
Having defeated the armies of Māra, he has attained supreme perfect enlightenment;
with the three types of omniscience he shines alone, his six supernormal powers are unimpeded,
and he is endowed with great compassion and inexhaustible eloquence.
All those to whom he proclaims [the Dharma] believe and accept it;
he expounds the subtle and wondrous Dharma to rescue and deliver all living beings.
Just as a vajra is capable of shattering whatever it is aimed at,
so too is the gateway of the Tathāgata’s teaching;
it can extinguish the afflictions and all fetters of sentient beings.
He traveled throughout the lands, villages, towns, and cities,
uprooting the thorns of affliction with the pure Dharma,
subduing those of external teachings, and establishing the supreme banner of victory.
Having closed the gates to the evil realms and opened the path to nirvāṇa,
and with his work of transforming sentient beings nearing completion, he was about to enter parinirvāṇa.
He addressed his great disciple Mahākāśyapa:
You should now know that for immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas,
I have diligently practiced austerities for the sake of sentient beings,
single-mindedly and exclusively seeking the unsurpassed, supreme Dharma.
"My former vows have now been fulfilled.
Kāśyapa, you should know that it is like dense clouds pervading the entire world."
Just as sweet rain falls and causes sprouts to grow,
so too is the unsurpassed rain of the Dharma;
it enables sentient beings to increase the seeds of their roots of goodness.
For this reason, all Buddhas constantly bestow upon you their protection, respect, praise, prostrations, and offerings;
even as I am now about to enter parinirvāṇa,
I entrust this profound Dharma to you.
"You should, in the future, respectfully follow my intention and widely proclaim and disseminate [this teaching] so that it does not become extinct. Kāśyapa replied:
Excellent! We shall receive these instructions.
We will uphold the True Dharma in this manner so that those in future ages may likewise receive its benefit.
I only pray that the World-Honored One will not be concerned.
Therefore, after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa,
Mahākāśyapa shall successively proclaim the true teaching.
He compiled the treasury of the Buddha’s Dharma to transform all sentient beings;
those whom he delivered shall never again fall back.
That Mahākāśyapa possesses wisdom as deep and vast as an ocean.
His fame is universally renowned and he is fully endowed with merit;
I shall now explain his conduct and vows accordingly.
Long ago in the past, there was the Buddha Vipaśyin.
Having transformed sentient beings, he entered parinirvāṇa.
The fourfold assembly of disciples, filled with grief and longing,
collected his relics and erected a stupa made of the seven precious substances.
The stupa’s spire and its adornments were exceptionally magnificent and exquisite.
Within that stupa was an image of the Tathāgata,
the golden color of whose face was slightly marred by a small area of damage.
At that time, there was a poor woman who wandered about begging and obtained a single golden bead;
she harbored great joy within her heart and intended to use it to patch a small area on the face of the image.
At that time, Kāśyapa was a goldsmith.
The girl took [the materials] and went to him, requesting his services for the construction.
Then, the goldsmith heard that she was performing meritorious deeds.
Delighted, she repaired it; once the polishing and ornamentation were complete, she used it to restore the face of the image, and they made a vow together, saying:
"May the two of us always be husband and wife."
His body was of a true golden color and he constantly experienced supreme bliss.
By virtue of these causes and conditions,
for ninety-one kalpas his body remained of a true golden color.
He experienced boundless happiness among humans and devas.
Finally, he took rebirth in the seventh Brahma-heaven.
At that time, in the kingdom of Magadha, there was a brahmin named Nikūludāya.
In past lives, he long cultivated superior deeds;
he was of lofty talent and broad erudition, with profound wisdom,
and possessed immeasurable wealth and vast riches.
Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, conch shells, jade, oxen,
sheep, fields, houses, slaves, and carriages—
these were a thousand times superior to those of King Magadha.
At that time, King Bimbisāra possessed one thousand ploughs;
fearing that he might incur various offenses by being equal to the king,
that brāhmaṇa reduced his number by one, so that he had only nine hundred and ninety-nine.
In that house there was fine cotton cloth;
even the lowest quality was worth a hundred thousand taels of gold.
He drove a nail into it so that it entered the earth to a depth of seven feet.
The cotton cloth was not torn or worn through, remaining no different than it had been originally.
Such was the extent of his wealth through the power of his merit;
yet, despite his abundant riches and treasures, he had no offspring.
Reflecting that he was aged and the time of his death was approaching,
and having no one to whom he could entrust the various goods in his storehouse,
he saw a tree-spirit by the side of his house.
That brahmin, seeking a son, went there to offer prayers;
yet after the passage of years, no sign of response appeared at all.
At that time, Kūṭadanta became greatly incensed and spoke to the tree deity, saying:
"I have served you for many years,
yet I have never seen you bestow even a single blessing upon me.
Today, for seven days, I shall serve you with a devoted heart."
"If there is no further proof, they will surely burn and cut me down.
Having heard this, the tree spirit was filled with great sorrow and fear,
and she related these matters in detail to the Four Heavenly Kings.
Thereupon, the Four Kings went to inform Śakra.
Śakra observed that within Jambudvīpa there was no person of sufficient merit and virtue to serve as his son;
he then proceeded to the Brahmā King and extensively proclaimed the aforementioned matter.
At that time, the Brahmā King, observing with his divine eye that a certain Brahmā deity was about to reach the end of his life,
immediately addressed him, saying:
"If you descend as a spirit..."
"It would be fitting for you to be born in that realm of Jambudvīpa into a brahmin family.
Brahmā replied, "The dharma of the brahmins abounds in evil and false views."
"I am currently unable to act as his son.
The Brahma King spoke again:
"That Brahmin possesses great majestic power."
"The people of Jambudvīpa are unable to endure rebirth there;
you must be born in that realm. I shall protect you with my own hands, ensuring that you never fall into wrong views."
Brahmā replied, "So be it," and respectfully accepted the holy teaching.
Thereupon, Śakra immediately spoke these matters to the tree deity.
The tree deity, filled with joy, immediately went to his house and said to the brahmin,
"Do not harbor resentment toward me any longer.
Seven days from now, your wish shall be fulfilled."
When the seventh day had passed, the wife realized she was pregnant;
when the ten months were fully completed, she gave birth to a son whose countenance was upright and handsome, and whose body was of a true golden color.
The radiance was brilliant and majestic, illuminating an area of one yojana.
A physiognomist divined and said:
"This child possesses great majestic power due to his accumulated merit from past lives."
His will and strength were pure and far-reaching, and he did not crave worldly affairs;
he would surely leave the household life to attain the fruit of non-attachment.
Although his years were those of a mere child, his aspirations were pure, and he practiced compassion and extensive giving.
Having few desires and being content, he constantly observed that worldly pleasures are impermanent, precarious, and fragile;
he never for a moment conceived a thought of attachment or delight toward them.
At that time, his parents saw him in this state.
Deeply distressed and sorrowful,
they said to one another,
"When this child was born..."
The physiognomist divined and said,
"He will certainly leave the household life.
Now, what means can be devised to sever this intention?"
He reflected to himself:
"That which people in this world can become attached to is nothing but beautiful form.
I must select a handsome and virtuous mate for her in order to sever her desire."
When he reached the age of fifteen and his parents wished to betroth him a wife,
Kāśyapa heard of this and was deeply distressed.
He spoke to his parents, saying:
"My aspiration is pure; I have no need for a wife.
Thus he spoke three times, yet his parents would not listen.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa realized that the matter could not be avoided.
He then devised a stratagem and said to his parents:
"Only when you can obtain for me a woman of golden complexion whose beauty surpasses that of the world shall I then set my mind at ease and accept her."
"If I do not find [such a woman], I shall never marry.
At that time, out of respect and consideration for him, his parents did not go against his word.
They immediately summoned various Brahmins and dispatched them to travel throughout the kingdom.
"If there is a woman whose body is of true golden color, upright, dignified, and exquisite, betroth her to me.
Thereupon, the brahmins deliberated together.
They cast a golden figure with extraordinary features and carried it together through various villages,
proclaiming aloud:
If there is a woman who sees this Golden Deity and pays him homage and makes offerings,
she will in the future certainly attain a body of subtle, wondrous wisdom and a true golden color.
Upon hearing this, all the women came forth to pay their respects.
Among them was one woman whose countenance was exquisite and whose body was the color of purple gold;
she was gentle by nature and possessed profound wisdom.
She was none other than the daughter Jin-zhu (Golden Pearl) of former days.
Because of past superior conditions, she possesses this wondrous body;
her resolve is firm and steadfast, such that she alone does not go outside.
The women all asked the reason for her refusal to come out.
She replied, "Sisters, my mind is tranquil and secluded; I do not desire any other aspiration."
Therefore, she did not come out.
At that time, the women forcibly took this girl to go and see the Golden Deity.
This girl’s radiance, form, and features were exquisite and beautiful.
The radiance of the Golden Deity was completely eclipsed so that it no longer appeared.
The brahmins then arranged for her marriage,
and they all gave their consent.
They calculated the date for their marriage;
when she heard of this, she was also deeply distressed.
Unable to follow her own will, she immediately went to be wed.
The two faced one another with their respective wills focused and pure;
though they were husband and wife, they were entirely devoid of carnal desire.
Together they established a covenant, saying:
"We should now each occupy separate rooms and not disturb one another.
When the parents learned of this matter,
they immediately ordered people to remove one of the chambers.
He had them stay together in a room that was cleared out, leaving only a single bed inside.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa made a further agreement with his wife:
"In this room now there is only one bed."
"It is not right for the two of us to sleep together.
If I rest and sleep, you should practice walking meditation;
if you lie down and sleep, I shall practice walking meditation."
Later, during the middle watch of the night, Kāśyapa went next;
his wife was then fast asleep with her hand hanging down in front of the bed.
A venomous snake from outside entered through the door, intending to bite her.
Kāśyapa, out of compassion, slowly approached;
he wrapped his hands in his robe and lifted [the child] to place him upon the bed.
His wife then woke up in alarm and reproached him, saying:
"Now, you man, to have such a lack of resolve!
Having made a vow with me that we would not approach one another,
for what reason do you now secretly raise your hand toward me?"
Kāśyapa replied,
"I have no lustful desire; it was a snake that entered from outside."
I intended to sting you,
fearing it might cause you harm;
I have merely raised my hand.
The poisonous snake was still there, so he showed it to her.
His wife’s mind was then awakened;
thereupon, husband and wife felt a profound weariness with all conditioned existence (*bhava*) and no longer took pleasure in them.
Just as a person who has washed themselves clean takes no pleasure in dust and grime,
he went to his parents and requested to leave the household life;
having received their permission, he then became a śramaṇa.
Pure and maintaining his simple nature, he was without action or desire;
dwelling in seclusion, he diligently practiced asceticism.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa made this vow:
"I take refuge in all those in the world who have become arhats.
Having spoken these words, he became fully endowed with all the precepts and the dignified deportment of one who has left the household life.
When the Tathāgata had attained all-knowledge and proclaimed the sublime Dharma in the city of Rājagṛha,
at that time Kāśyapa, wearing rag-robes,
approached the Buddha’s presence, prostrated himself in salutation, stood with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
World-Honored One,
I now take refuge in the unsurpassed coolness.
I pray that you will compassionately accept me and allow me to stand at the very end of the assembly.
The World-Honored One praised him, saying,
"Welcome, Kāśyapa," and immediately divided his seat in half, commanding him to sit.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"I am but a junior disciple of the Tathāgata;
though you command me to share your seat, I dare not comply with your wish."
At that time, the entire assembly conceived a doubt, saying:
"What extraordinary virtue does this old śramaṇa possess,
such that the World-Honored One has offered him half of his seat?"
The superiority of this person is known only to the Buddha. Thereupon,
the Tathāgata, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly and their desire to resolve their doubts,
proclaimed the profound and vast great conduct of Kāśyapa.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"I am now adorned with great loving-kindness, great compassion, the four dhyānas, samādhi, and immeasurable merits;
the bhikṣu Kāśyapa is likewise so adorned."
Furthermore, in the distant past, long ago,
there was a noble king named Mandhātṛ,
whose lofty talent transcended the world and whose wisdom was peerless.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, in admiration of his virtue,
sent a chariot of the seven treasures and constructed a gate to welcome the king.
Thereupon, he mounted the celestial chariot and traveled through the air.
The Heavenly King came out to welcome him and sat together with him.
After they had enjoyed each other’s company, he escorted the King back to his palace.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
At that time, the Lord of Devas was none other than the present Kāśyapa; King Mandhātṛ was myself.
In the past, Kāśyapa invited me to sit together upon the seat of birth and death.
Therefore, on this day, I have attained the Unsurpassed Way and repay his original merit by means of the Seat of the True Dharma.
At that time, the World-Honored One [spoke] thus for Kāśyapa.
He taught the Dharma as was appropriate, instructing, exhorting, benefiting,
and gladdening them; just as fresh, pure white cotton easily takes dye,
they attained arhatship right there on their seats.
He possessed the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
Of lofty talent and courageous spirit, his demeanor was serene and composed;
he constantly sat facing the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma.
At that time, the devas and humans regarded the World-Honored One as their teacher.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa took his leave of the Tathāgata and went to the Piṇḍava Cave on Vulture Peak Mountain.
That mountain abounds with flowing springs and bathing pools;
its forests are lush and verdant, and its flowers and fruits are abundant.
A hundred beasts roam and gather there, while auspicious birds soar and sing.
Gold, silver, and lapis lazuli were spread across its ground.
There, Kāśyapa practiced walking meditation and contemplation,
proclaiming the sublime Dharma to deliver all sentient beings.
Later, when the World-Honored One was about to enter parinirvāṇa,
he emitted a supreme radiance and the great earth shook;
thereupon, he formed this thought:
"Could it be that the Tathāgata, wishing to enter parinirvāṇa, has manifested this sign?
He immediately entered samādhi and observed with his divine eye,
seeing that the World-Honored One had relinquished his life-span in his entirety on the banks of the Hiraṇyavatī River.
Having made this observation, he was deeply distressed and displeased, thinking:
"How swiftly the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa has come!
The eye of the world is extinguished, and unwholesomeness increases."
Accompanied by his retinue surrounding him before and behind,
he proceeded toward the city of Kuśinagara to pay homage to the World-Honored One.
On the road ahead, he encountered a brahmin.
Holding a *mandārava* flower in his right hand,
Kāśyapa asked him,
"From where have you come?"
"Do you know my teacher? He replied, "I do.
It has already been seven days since he entered parinirvāṇa."
"All the humans and devas have made a grand offering.
I obtained these flowers from among them.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they were moved.
Filled with great compassion and distress, they threw their entire bodies to the ground;
wailing and sobbing, tears fell like rain as they all spoke these words:
Alas! Impermanence possesses such great power that it can destroy this precious accumulation of merit,
dry up the ocean of Dharma, and topple the banner of the Dharma.
The world is shrouded in darkness, having forever lost its great illumination;
all sentient beings have nothing to revere or look up to;
the evil realms increase while the devas and humans diminish.
How marvelous that impermanence is so deeply loathsome!
Like a flash of lightning, it has no principle of lasting long;
impermanence is so swift that it is difficult even to preserve.
It can destroy the vigor, beauty, and lifespan of one's prime;
it utterly extinguishes all worldly joy and affection.
Fools cherish it, but the wise do not.
Thereupon, Kāśyapa and the bhikṣus proceeded forward to the space between the twin trees;
they circumambulated the coffin three times and prostrated themselves in salutation.
And he spoke in verse:
"Transcending the triple world, you ride upon the vehicle; Forever crossing the stream of birth and death, Tranquil, signless, and wishless— Subtle, wondrous, and inconceivable."
The Buddha-sun is most bright and pure, capable of dispelling the darkness of ignorance;
having cultivated ascetic practices through many eons, you vowed to deliver all suffering beings—
why then, at this time, do you abandon great compassion?
Your entire body rests within the golden coffin, Tranquil, peaceful,
and unmoving. I pray that you, Honored One among gods and humans, Reveal your golden-hued body,
Causing all sentient beings everywhere To give rise to immeasurable vows.
At that time, from within the golden coffin and amidst the thousand layers of fine cotton cloth, the World-Honored One extended his golden feet;
their radiance shone brilliantly like the midday sun,
yet the coffin and the cloth remained unimpaired as the feet were revealed.
When the entire assembly saw this, their grief and distress redoubled; they wailed and sobbed until their voices were choked with emotion.
At that time, Kāśyapa bared his right shoulder, touched [the Buddha's] feet, and paid homage.
He spoke again in verse:
"The Tathāgata’s ankles are full; The thousand-spoked wheels appear on his feet;
His fingers are slender, long, and soft; And he is endowed with webbed hands."
With great compassion you rescue all living beings and sever the knots of doubt in the world;
therefore, on this day, I prostrate at the feet of the Most Victorious One.
Having realized the Four Noble Truths, I shall proclaim the mass of the Buddha’s virtues.
Having offered praise and reverence, it was fitting to withdraw one’s feet and enter.
At that time, Kāśyapa had the Mallas further wrap the Buddha’s body with a thousand layers of fine cotton cloth.
Having poured fragrant oil over [the body], they closed the coffin lid.
They piled up sandalwood fuel and cremated the Tathāgata.
Seeing the fire, Ānanda wept with sorrow, choking with sobs, wailing and lamenting in distress.
And he spoke these verses:
"How strange is impermanence! It is truly a cause for deep sorrow and fear, For it can extinguish such a treasury of precious virtues— This body of the World-Honored One, Pure and stainless."
Now he lies within a golden coffin, wrapped in a thousand layers of fine cotton cloth;
fragrant oil flows over it as sandalwood fuel burns. Where is that subtle and supreme body?
At that time, Kāśyapa—
He extinguished the fire with milk and spoke this verse in praise:
"Though his body were wrapped in a thousand layers of cotton and set ablaze, by the Buddha’s spiritual power— "
"One garment remained inside, and even the exterior was not burned; only the middle part was completely consumed—such is this supreme spiritual power, inconceivable.
Having spoken this verse, Mahākāśyapa addressed the bhikṣus:
The Buddha has already been cremated.
The remains of the World-Honored One are not our concern. Why is this?
"Kings, elders, ministers, and householders will seek the most supreme merit and should themselves provide offerings.
We ought now to compile the Eye of the Dharma."
Do not allow the torch of the Dharma to perish so quickly; rather,
act as a source of illumination for future generations,
ensuring that the Three Jewels are sustained and never severed.
At that time, Kāśyapa and the bhikṣus went to the Piṇḍava Cave in Rājagṛha;
King Ajātaśatru attained groundless faith.
When the Tathāgata had entered parinirvāṇa, the ministers deliberated together, saying:
"The Great King’s faith was like a vast ocean,
surpassing all the worlds of humans and devas."
If he were to hear that the World-Honored One has entered parinirvāṇa,
boiling blood would surely flow from his face;
his body would fall apart, and his life would not last much longer.
"What means should be devised to escape this calamity?
At that time, there was a minister named Vṛṣṇa,
whose wisdom was profound and vast, and who was skilled in expedient means.
Construct a bronze pool several fathoms in length and breadth,
fill its interior with pure fragrant oil,
and cause King Ajātaśatru to sit within this pool.
Furthermore, one should use fresh, pure white cotton cloth to depict an image of the Tathāgata’s past conduct— specifically,
the Bodhisattva descending from Tuṣita Heaven, miraculously riding a white elephant, and entering the womb of his mother.
His father was named Śuddhodana and his mother was called Māyā.
He was born after a full ten months in the womb;
as soon as he was born and had not yet reached the ground, Śakra received him.
The Dragon Kings Nanda and Upananda spouted water to bathe him,
while the Great Ghost King Maṇibhadra held a precious parasol and stood in attendance behind him.
The Earth Goddess manifested flowers to receive his feet.
He walked seven paces in each of the four directions.
Upon reaching a celestial temple, he caused all the images of the devas to rise and welcome him.
The seer Asita took him in his arms and performed a physiognomic divination.
Having completed the divination, he was overcome with great sorrow and suffering,
lamenting that he would not live to witness the appearance of a Buddha.
He went to his teacher to study calligraphy, the arts, and prophetic diagrams;
while dwelling in the deep palace, he enjoyed pleasures with sixty thousand court ladies.
He went out of the city to travel and observe, arriving at the Kapilavastu Garden.
On the way, he saw an old man and a śramaṇa;
upon returning to the palace, he saw the various court ladies,
whose bodies and features were like withered bones.
There was no difference between his palaces and his tombs; loathing them,
he left the household life at midnight, leaped over the city walls,
and went to the great seers such as Udraka Rāmaputra and Ārāḍa Kālāma.
Having heard the teachings on the sphere of consciousness and the attainment of neither-perception-nor-non-perception,
and having heard this, he investigated them with profound discernment,
knowing them to be impermanent, suffering, impure, and non-self.
Having abandoned his six years of ascetic practice under the tree,
he realized that such suffering could not lead to the Way.
At that time, he went again to the river Ārīṭṭhakī to bathe.
At that time, there were two cowherd women who,
wishing to make an offering to a deity, milked one thousand cows to provide milk for five hundred;
they continued this process in succession until it reached a single cow.
He immediately took that milk and boiled it to make gruel;
it surged nine feet high without losing a single drop.
A brahmin asked him, saying:
"Sister, for whom do you intend to serve this porridge?
The woman replied immediately:
He was maintaining the tree deity for the sacrifice. A Brahmin asked,
"What deity is there capable of receiving this food?"
"Only one who possesses all-encompassing wisdom (sarvajñā) can partake of such an offering as yours. Thereupon,
the woman presented it to the Bodhisattva.
He immediately accepted it and consumed it;
only then did he proceed to the foot of the Bodhi tree,
where he defeated Māra Pāpīyas and attained supreme perfect enlightenment.
From turning the Wheel of Dharma for the first time at Vārāṇasī for the five bhikṣus,
until arriving at the city of Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas, where he entered parinirvāṇa.
All such images as these were depicted there.
The king asked his ministers, "What have you done?"
He replied, "Great King,
I painted an image of the Tathāgata’s meritorious qualities;
next, I depicted the transformation of the World-Honored One’s form at his parinirvāṇa."
The king was struck with such astonishment that the hair on his entire body stood on end;
he felt a profound sense of sorrowful longing and yearned for the Tathāgata.
One-fifth of the oil in this pool—
Suddenly it flowed and entered the King's body,
just as when a piece of burnt brick is thrown into a great pool, the water naturally seeps into it; so it was with him.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, his life was fully saved.
King Ajātaśatru’s faith and reverence became so profound that his longing for the Tathāgata was as great as this.
Upon hearing that Kāśyapa was coming, he was filled with great joy;
he prepared the roads by burning incense and scattering flowers,

forever leave behind all suffering, and attain the bliss of nirvāṇa.
Kāśyapa next entrusted me, my teacher Ānanda;
Ānanda in turn further charged me with this responsibility.
Now that I wish to enter parinirvāṇa, I entrust it to you.
If you should wish for parinirvāṇa in the future,
there shall appear in the world a son of good family in the kingdom of Mathurā.
His name is Tīrṭika;
having long cultivated vows and practices, his eloquence is inexhaustible.
You should, in the future, deliver him and cause him to leave the household life.
"You may entrust them all to him with the Dharma-eye.
Upagupta replied, "So be it;
I shall receive your instruction."
When he reached the Venerable Upagupta,

however, he observed that Tiṣya had not yet appeared in the world.
Reflecting upon this, he realized that [the Dharma] had not yet appeared in the world.
At that time, the Venerable Upagupta, leading a community of bhikṣus, went to his house;
gradually the number diminished until he was alone.
His father, the elder, asked:
"Great Sage, do you have no retinue? Why do you travel alone?"
Upagupta replied, "Householder,
we who have left the household life have no one to serve us."
"If there is anyone [who can help], please grant us your favor.
The elder spoke again:
"I delight in living at home and cannot practice the Way.
If later I bear a son, I shall surely provide for you. Upagupta said:
"Excellent is this intention!
You should maintain this mind and not allow it to change or regret.
Furthermore, this elder has fathered many sons."
All the children died at a very young age;
finally, a son was born named Tiṭṭibha,

He was well able to receive and study various treatises, sūtras, and records.
Having deeply planted roots of goodness through his past cultivation,
Upagupta went to him to seek them.
The elder, filled with joy, personally handed him over.
He took him to the monastery, ordained him as a novice,

At the time of the first proclamation, one severs the fetters of the truths and attains the stage of Srotāpanna.
At the first *karmavācanā*, with the thinning of lust, anger, and delusion, one attains the stage of Sakṛdāgāmin.
At the second *karmavācanā*, with the exhaustion of the fetters of the desire realm, one attains the stage of Anāgāmin.
At the moment of the third *karmavācanā*, he severed the afflictions of the three realms,
established the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and became an Arhat.
With the three knowledges (*vidyā*) shining afar and the six supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) fully perfected.
He moved about with mastery, appearing and disappearing without obstruction.
Upagupta then addressed him, saying, "The World-Honored One,
the Sun of Wisdom, covers all with his great compassion."
Desiring to rescue sentient beings from the great suffering of birth and death,
he entrusted the Dharma accumulated over immeasurable kalpas to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
Acting as a great bright lamp to illuminate the darkness of ignorance for all,
may you cause everyone everywhere to practice and learn,
severing the net of craving and emerging from the mire of desire.
Kāśyapa next entrusted it to the bhikṣu Ānanda.
After Ānanda’s parinirvāṇa, he charged my teacher Śāṇakavāsin with it.
Śāṇakavāsin, in turn, entrusted it to me.

sprinkling the flavor of ambrosia to heal the thirst of afflictions; yet,
for me now, that which was to be done has been accomplished.
The time for my parinirvāṇa has arrived; my final liberation is not far off.
I entrust this Dharma-treasure to you.
Hereafter, you should receive, uphold, and honor it upon the crown of your head.
Exert yourself to guard it diligently so that it is not lost or leaked away;
spread the light of the Dharma to illuminate the darkness of ignorance.
Furthermore, O Udāyī.
When the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa and the noble sages have vanished,

the ten thousand Abhidharma-piṭakas and the eighty thousand pure Vinayas—
all such dharmas as these will likewise gradually diminish.

how much more so when many noble sages all pass into extinction together,
such that the pure, wondrous, and supreme Dharma will forever leave nothing remaining.
Therefore, I now earnestly entrust this to you. You should,
with a sincere heart, respectfully comply with my intent and give rise to thoughts of great compassion toward all sentient beings.
"Receive, uphold, and propagate [this] so that it shall not be interrupted.

Acting as uninvited friends for future generations,

those whom he transformed and delivered were exceedingly vast and extensive.
When the causal conditions were exhausted and he entered nirvana, humans and devas were moved by grief;
they immediately collected his relics and erected a stupa made of the seven precious substances,
making various offerings by burning incense and scattering flowers.
In the past, when Tīṣya was approaching his parinirvāṇa,
he entrusted the Dharma to his greatest disciple, named Miśraka.

he then addressed him, saying,
"The Buddha has entrusted the True Dharma to Mahākāśyapa."
In this manner, it was passed down successively until it reached me.
As I am about to enter parinirvāṇa, I entrust it to you.
You shall later propagate this Eye of the World throughout the world, Mithyaka, so say.
"Excellent! We shall receive these instructions.

Thereupon, he proclaimed and disseminated the precious treasury of the True Dharma, causing all sentient beings to open the path to Nirvana. Having completed his work of transformation through conditions, he was about to enter parinirvāṇa.
Furthermore, he entrusted the True Dharma next to the Venerable Buddhanandi,
commanding him to disseminate the supreme flavor of ambrosia.
Subsequently, Nandi extensively proclaimed and analyzed it, turning the Great Wheel of Dharma and subduing the enmity of Māra.
Thereafter, he entrusted [the teaching] to Buddhamitra.
That person’s power of virtue was profoundly deep and immeasurable;
through skillful means, he transformed and guided all sentient beings.
Causing them to leave behind evil views and enter the most supreme path;
adorning themselves with great wisdom,
they expound the flavor of purity and utterly destroy the heterodox teachings.
Such merits are inexhaustible;
I shall now describe a small portion of them in accordance with the truth.
There was a great king who ruled over the entire world.
Though possessed of high talent, courage, extensive learning, and broad erudition,
he followed heterodox teachings and accepted false views;
he constantly harbored contempt and disparagement for the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
Buddhamitra thought to himself:
"My teacher Nandi has entrusted the Dharma to me;
how shall I expound this supreme eye?"
He caused all sentient beings to obtain universal benefit.
Then he further thought:
"Now this king possesses extremely great wrong views."
I should go there first and subdue him;
it is like felling a tree—
if one topples its root.
"How could branches, leaves, flowers, and stems endure for long?
Having formed this thought,
he personally carried a crimson banner for twelve years, walking before the king.
For a long time the King did not inquire about him;
only after this period had passed did he suddenly ask,
"Who is this person walking before me?"
He was summoned immediately and questioned about his intentions.
He replied, "Great King,
I am a man of wisdom who is skilled in discourse."
He wished to request a trial before the king.
At that time, the Great King immediately issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom for all brahmins, elders, and householders who were intelligent, erudite, and skilled in speech.
"Let all of you assemble in my Palace of Supreme Victory to engage in debate with a śramaṇa. Thereupon,
all those heterodox practitioners of wrong views gathered.
Possessing profound eloquence and vast, penetrating wisdom,
he was thoroughly versed in all matters of celestial phenomena and terrestrial geography. Yet,
those harboring hearts of malice and venom vied with one another to assemble like clouds.
At that time, the great king, within his main hall,
prepared and arranged offerings, spreading out carpets and mats;
he burned incense and scattered flowers, making the place magnificent, bright, and pure.
Buddhamitra then ascended the Dharma seat and engaged with the various non-Buddhists in a debate on boundless doctrines;
those of shallow intelligence were defeated by him with a single word.
That man, being highly eloquent and possessing consummate skill in debate,
exhausted the arguments of all the others. Seeing that everyone else had reached the end of their reasoning,
the King personally engaged Maitreya in discussion.
As soon as he began to speak, his arguments were immediately refuted.
Buddhajīva then thought to himself:
"It is not appropriate for me to display my superiority in debate with the king."
He spoke to him, saying,
"The depth or shallowness of this meaning the King will understand for himself.
At that time, the King immediately recognized his own defeat.
They turned away from their deviant minds and came to reverently believe in the True Dharma;
they received the three refuges and became disciples of the Buddha,
widely proclaiming the transformative teachings of the Way within their own lands.
At that time, there was in this country a Nirgrantha whose false views were rampant; he slandered the True Dharma,
yet was eloquent, wise, and highly proficient in calculation.
Because the Buddha Maitreya wished to transform him,
he went to become his disciple and received this art from him;
before long, through study and practice, he mastered it entirely.
That Nirgrantha let out a great, malicious cry and reviled the Buddha.
Then, Buddharakṣita said to the Nirgrantha:
Do not utter such words,
lest you incur sin;
as a retribution for this, you shall surely fall into the great hell.
The Nirgrantha said,
"How could you possibly know such a matter?
Maitreya replied:
"If you do not believe me, you may calculate it for yourself;
once you have calculated it, you will know it for yourself.
Thereupon, that Nirgrantha proceeded to perform the calculation.
Upon seeing that his body was certain to fall into hell,
he was immediately seized by great terror and gave rise to profound remorse.
He prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before Maitreya.
He addressed him, saying,
"O Benevolent One, how may I avoid this transgression? Buddhamitra replied:
"Nirgrantha,
it is like one who has fallen to the ground because of the earth;
if you take refuge in the Buddha, this transgression may be extinguished."
At that time, the Nirgrantha conceived great faith and praised the Tathāgata with five hundred verses;
he repented of his former transgressions and severely reproached himself.
The Buddha Maitreya then addressed him, saying:
"By virtue of the causes and conditions of this wholesome karma of your mind, you shall certainly be reborn in the heavens after your life ends. The Nirgrantha spoke again:
"How do you know that I have been reborn in heaven? Maitreya replied,
"If you do not believe me, calculate it yourself to find the truth."
At that time, the Nirgrantha immediately performed the calculations and saw for himself that his own sins were extinguished and he was reborn in heaven.
He was filled with great joy and sought compassionate permission to leave the household life. Maitreya replied,
"On this day, you should inform your kinsmen."
"Only then shall I consider ordaining you.
There were five hundred disciples of the Nirgrantha;
he went to their place and said to them:
I have perceived the supreme truth and my heart feels profound love and joy for it.
I wish to leave the household life to practice the Way within the Buddha-dharma. You may now act as you desire.
Furthermore, he received instruction from a brilliant master and consulted him to receive the sublime Dharma.
At that time, all the disciples addressed the master, saying:
"We have fundamentally looked up to you with reverence, like a great canopy of clouds."
As the Master entered the path of supreme resolve,
those five hundred Nirgranthas followed him to the place of the Venerable One and all went forth together into the religious life.
Thereupon, the venerable Buddhagupta’s melodious voice spread throughout Jambudvīpa,
and he brought immeasurable sentient beings to spiritual transformation.
When his life came to an end, his disciples were filled with grief;
they collected his relics and erected a stupa to make offerings to them.
Long ago, there was the Venerable Buddharmitra.
When his work for the sake of sentient beings was completed and he was about to relinquish his life,
he addressed a disciple named the bhikṣu Pārśva: "You shall,
hereafter, extensively propagate the holy teaching."
He transformed all sentient beings, causing them to attain liberation.
He addressed the Great Master, saying,
"I respectfully receive your venerable instruction."
"I shall, with a sincere heart, protect the True Dharma.
That monk Pārśva, due to his past karma,
remained within his mother's womb for more than sixty years."
After he was born, his beard and hair turned white;
loathing the five desires and finding no pleasure in living at home,
he went to seek out the Venerable Buddhamitra.
He prostrated at his feet and requested to enter the ranks of the Path.
He was immediately ordained and the Dharma essentials were taught to him;
it was like a fresh, pure white cotton cloth that easily takes on dye.
Thereupon, while seated upon his mat, he attained the path of Arhatship;
the three insights (vidyā) shone through him clearly, and his six supernormal powers (abhijñā) were unimpeded.
He diligently practiced asceticism with fierce and courageous vigor.
He never lay down to sleep with his side touching the ground;
thus, people of the time called him the "Side-Bhikṣu.
He skillfully expounded the essentials of the Dharma to transform all sentient beings.
Having completed what was to be done, he entered parinirvāṇa;
his relics were collected and a stūpa was erected for worship.
That Bhikṣu Pārśva was on the verge of passing into extinction.
He addressed a bhikṣu named Pūrṇaśa, saying: "Venerable one,
you should know that the Buddha-dharma is subtle and wondrous, possessing great merit."
For this reason, all the noble ones receive and uphold it upon their heads.
I have received this entrustment and shall protect this Dharma;
now, as I am about to enter parinirvāṇa, I leave it to you as my legacy.
"You should protect and uphold this with a sincere mind.
Then Pūrṇaśa replied, "So be it."
Thereupon, he expounded the subtle and supreme Dharma,
thereby transforming and delivering immeasurable sentient beings.
Later, on one occasion, while staying beneath a secluded grove, he [was visited].
Sitting in the full lotus posture, he meditated in profound stillness.
There was a great being named Aśvaghoṣa,
whose wisdom was deep and discerning, and whose superior insight was beyond compare.
In all his challenging questions, there was nothing he did not crush and subdue;
it was like a fierce wind blowing down and uprooting rotten wood,
or raising a great cloud of arrogance over sentient beings who were as insignificant as blades of grass and chaff.
I had falsely imagined that there was a self and was exceedingly arrogant;
however, I have heard that there is a venerable one named Pūrṇaśa,
whose wisdom is profound and who is widely learned and erudite.
They say that all phenomena are empty, devoid of self,
and devoid of persons; yet, harboring a mind of contempt,
they approach them and speak these words:
Whatever discourses exist in all the worlds,
I am able to destroy them like hail crushing grass;
if these words were false and not truthful, [may such-and-such calamity befall me].
"One must surely cut off one's tongue to atone for such an offense. Pūrṇaśa said,
"Within the Buddha-dharma, there are generally two truths."
If one speaks of a "self" as a conventional designation according to worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*),
then in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) all things are entirely empty and quiescent.
When investigated in this manner, how could a self ever be found?
At that time, Aśvaghoṣa’s mind was not yet subdued;
relying on his own sharp intelligence, he still considered himself superior.
Pūrṇa said to him:
"Reflect carefully; do not speak falsely.
I shall now determine with you who is the victor.
Thereupon, Aśvaghoṣa thought to himself:
The conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is established as merely a provisional designation and is certainly not real;
the nature of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is likewise empty and quiescent.
Thus, both of these two truths are ultimately unattainable.
Since there is nothing at all that can be destroyed, how could I possibly do so?
I am certainly no match for him now;
I wish instead to cut out my own tongue to apologize for this humiliation.
Pūrṇa said, "My Dharma is compassionate; I shall not cut off your tongue.
You should shave your head and become my disciple."
At that time, the Venerable One ordained him as a monk.
His mind was still filled with remorse and resentment, and he desired to give up his life. Then Pūrṇa attained the path of an Arhat;
entering meditative concentration, he observed and knew the thoughts in [the other's] mind.
The Venerable One had a sūtra previously left in a dark room;
he then sent Aśvaghoṣa to fetch it, and [Aśvaghoṣa] addressed him,
saying, "Great Master."
"This room is dark; how can one go there?
He replied, "Just go;
I shall cause you to see."
At that time, the Venerable One, by means of his supernormal power,
extended his right hand from afar into the interior of the room;
light radiated from his five fingers, its brilliance shining resplendently.
Everything within the room appeared clearly.
At that time, Aśvaghoṣa suspected in his mind that it was an illusion;
for any illusory phenomenon ceases once it is understood as such.
Yet this radiance grew even more intense;
though he exhausted all his skills in an attempt to extinguish it,
he became utterly weary without achieving any change in its appearance.
Recognizing what the Teacher had done, he immediately subdued himself and applied himself diligently to ascetic practices without ever turning back.
In this way, the Venerable One delivered all sentient beings through skillful means.
Having completed what was to be done, he entered nirvāṇa;
the fourfold assembly, moved by longing, erected a stūpa to make offerings.
Formerly, when Pūrṇaśa was on the verge of entering nirvāṇa...
He entrusted the Dharma to his disciple Aśvaghoṣa and addressed him, saying:
"It is like lighting a great bright lamp in a dark room."
All things are fully illuminated;
the lamp of the Dharma is likewise,
spreading throughout the world and able to extinguish the darkness of ignorance.
Therefore, the Tathāgata expounds this True Dharma so that all may universally practice it;
may all the worthy and holy ones constantly provide protection and guardianship.
I entrust this to you together with all others, even unto me;
I hold it fast with my supreme eye and now confer it upon you.
You should, in the future, receive and uphold it with a sincere heart.
"May all beings in future ages universally obtain benefit.
Aśvaghoṣa respectfully assented, saying, "I shall receive your venerable instruction," and thereupon proclaimed the profound treasury of the Dharma.
He erected the great banner of the Dharma to destroy and extinguish false views.
He traveled through and taught in the city of Pāṭaliputra,
desiring to deliver all sentient beings within that city.
They performed exquisite music called rathāvalī,
its sound pure, elegant, plaintive, and harmonious,
proclaiming the Dharma of suffering, emptiness, and non-self.
That which is called the conditioned is like an illusion or a magical transformation; this prison of the three realms has not a single thing worth delighting in.
Though a royal throne may be lofty and eminent, and its power sovereign, once impermanence arrives, who can remain?
Like clouds in the sky that vanish in an instant,
this body is false and deceptive, like a plantain tree;
it is an enemy and a thief, and should not be approached.
Like a basket containing a venomous snake, who would ever take pleasure in it?
For this reason, the Buddhas constantly revile this body.
Thus, they extensively explain the meaning of emptiness and non-self.
He commanded the musicians to perform this music,
but the performers were unable to comprehend it;
the melodies and rhythms were all performed incorrectly.
At that time, Aśvaghoṣa,
wearing white cotton garments, entered among the musicians;
he himself struck the bells and drums and tuned the lutes and harps.
The syllables were mournful and elegant, and the melodic tunes were perfectly formed;
he proclaimed all dharmas as suffering, empty, and selfless.
At that time, there were five hundred princes within this city.
Simultaneously, they attained awakening, came to loathe the five desires, and left the household life to pursue the Way.

At that time, the King of Pāṭaliputra feared that his people, upon hearing these sounds of joy, would abandon their homes; he worried that the kingdom would become desolate and the royal affairs would fall into ruin.
He even issued a proclamation to the people of that land, saying:
"From this day forward, do not perform such music again.
In that city of Pāṭaliputra, there were nine hundred million people in total.
The King of the Yuezhi was of majestic and flourishing virtue;
his name was King Candana-Kaniṣka.
His will and spirit were fierce and bold, and his valor and strength surpassed those of the world.
In all his military expeditions, there were none he did not crush and subdue.
He immediately arrayed the fourfold army and marched toward this land;
after engaging in mutual combat, they subsequently submitted and took refuge.
Even if he were to demand nine hundred million pieces of gold,
the king would immediately offer the horse Kanthaka and the compassionate chicken that brought the Buddha’s alms bowl,
each valued at three hundred million.
He took it and presented it to King Kaniṣka.
The Bodhisattva Aśvaghoṣa possessed preeminent wisdom,
and the Buddha’s bowl was endowed with merit such that it had been held by the Tathāgata himself.
This rooster possesses a heart of compassion and does not drink water containing insects;
it is capable of utterly destroying all enemies.
For these reasons, it is worth nine hundred million coins.
The King was greatly delighted and accepted him;
he immediately turned his troops back and returned to his own country.
That King of Kiṇṭhaka possessed great merit.
Donning the armor of the great vow with firm resolve,
he once placed a lump of clay upon a stupa and made this aspiration:
"If, in a future age among the number of the thousand Buddhas, I shall attain perfect enlightenment,
may this lump of clay be transformed into a Buddha image.
Having made this vow, it was immediately accomplished at that very moment.
The appearance of his majestic demeanor was extraordinary, as if depicted in a painting;
his heart was filled with immense joy and he leaped for joy beyond measure.
Later, the king was traveling along a road.
Seeing a stūpa of the non-Buddhists adorned with the seven precious jewels,
he was filled with great joy and, thinking it to be a stūpa of the Tathāgata,
went forward to prostrate himself, paid homage with a sincere heart, burned incense, scattered flowers, and praised it with a verse:
Endowed with all-encompassing wisdom, having severed the obstacles of desire and affliction,
the most supreme among the many seers; his fame pervades the three realms,
liberated and free from all states of existence, he takes pity upon all classes of living beings.
"What you have spoken is the true reality; it can topple the banner of false doctrines.
Therefore, I now pay homage to the Honored One, the Worthy One.
Having spoken this verse, the jeweled stupa immediately split apart and collapsed.
The king, seeing this, was struck with terror and spoke these words:
"Is my merit now about to be exhausted that I shall lose my royal throne?
For what reason has this precious stupa collapsed just as I have finished paying it homage?"
Someone said, "That which the King pays homage to is a heretical stūpa;
its majestic power is but meager and slight."
"One who is unworthy to receive the prostrations of a king’s merit is indeed such a person.
Having said this, he immediately opened the base of the stūpa and found the corpse of a Nirgrantha there.
The multitude sighed in admiration, saying:
How marvelous! The power of the Great King’s virtue is so profound that by paying homage to this heterodox stupa,
he has caused it to be destroyed.
The King’s merit was comparable to that of Brahmā.
Furthermore, on one occasion, Kaniṣka commanded his barber to shave his beard.
At that time, the barber stood before the king and spoke these words:
"My son is handsome and possesses rare wisdom;
I pray only that Your Majesty, out of compassion and pity, will grant him your daughter as his wife."
The king became greatly incensed and said to him:
"You are of low birth and inferior lineage;
how could my daughter become your wife?"
Even after being banished to another place,
he remained silent and did not dare speak again.
Later, when summoned once more, his words were just as they had been before.
Thus he repeated this three times.
The king reflected,
"There must certainly be a hidden treasure beneath this ground."
"Therefore, let this man dare to speak such words.
He immediately dispatched men to excavate the spot right then and there,
and they soon discovered a vast hoard of various treasures.
Such was the wisdom of the king.
Furthermore, on one occasion, Kaniṣka questioned his ministers:
"In the various kingdoms, is there any wise man whom we may consult and honor?"
At that time, there was a bhikṣu named Dharmamitra, whose wisdom was profound and far-reaching,
who was fully endowed with meritorious qualities,
and who was well-able to penetrate the characteristics of samādhi and meditative concentration.
In the kingdom of South India, there were two bhikṣus whose minds were gentle and mild, who deeply delighted in the sublime Dharma,
and who had long heard that the Venerable One was foremost in meditative concentration.
They then went together to that place.
At his dwelling were three tiers of caves;
at that time, the two men entered the lowest cave.
He saw a bhikṣu wearing tattered and worn-out robes,
his appearance ugly and unsightly, sitting upright before a hearth lighting a fire for the Saṃgha.
At that time, two bhikṣus asked him:
"Where is the Elder Dharmamitra? He replied,
"He is currently in the Supreme Cave."
"You all should go quickly to see him. At that time,
the two men proceeded to the upper cave and saw the aforementioned bhikṣu already seated within it.
Then a certain bhikṣu said to his companion,
"How is it that this old bhikṣu resembles the one we saw earlier?
At that time, the companion bhikṣu was wise and possessed of quick discernment.
He then said to him:
"Even this venerable one is now able to spread his fame in such a manner."
"How could you not come to this place and sit here?
He then stepped forward, paid his respects with a prostration, and asked:
"Venerable Sir, your majestic reputation is rare indeed in this world."
"Why have you humbled yourself to light a fire for the Saṃgha?
Dharmamitra said to the bhikṣu,
"Son, you should now listen."
I reflect that the suffering within birth and death has lasted for a long time.
If it were possible to burn my head and hands,
I would do so entirely for the sake of the Sangha.
How much less so for other parts of the body or for burning with fire—
what is there to find difficult?
I recall the past.
For five hundred lifetimes, he constantly took birth as a dog;
emaciated by hunger and destitute, he was able to eat his fill only twice.
This occurred in the past when he encountered a certain person.
Having drunk wine until intoxicated, they vomited and lay prostrate upon the ground; at that time, I ate my fill.
Furthermore, in the past, there was once a husband and wife.
When the gruel was cooked in the vessel, he went outside.
Seeing that no one had entered his house,
he put his head into the vessel and ate the gruel until he was satisfied.
Later, when he wished to emerge with his head, he was unable to do so.
Thereupon, the husband and wife returned from outside;
seeing that he had devoured their gruel, they felt deep resentment.
He immediately used a sharp blade to cut off my head;
for five hundred lifetimes, I suffered in the bodies of dogs,
and though we were twice satiated, we lost our lives.
Reflecting thus upon how birth and death are long-lasting and pervasive across the five realms, where one undergoes immeasurable suffering,
I now do not shrink from diligent toil;
I shall personally kindle a fire for the sake of the assembly of monks.
When the two bhikṣus heard these words,
they deeply contemplated the immeasurable faults and afflictions of birth and death,
and immediately attained the stage of srotāpanna.
Thus, the Venerable Dharmamitra was renowned for his lofty insight and vision, and his fame had spread far and wide;
